questions.question: A defendant loses in an Oregon circuit court, appeals to an intermediate court, and petitions the state's highest court, whose seven justices Oregonians elect statewide. Which sequence names her path and her final stop?
questions.correctAnswer: Circuit Court, then the Oregon Court of Appeals, then the Oregon Supreme Court - the state's court of last resort
distractors: Justice Court, then the Oregon Tax Court, then the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco
Circuit Court, then the Oregon Senate, then the U.S. Supreme Court directly
Municipal Court, then the Court of Appeals, then the governor's pardon board
questions.explanation: Oregon's trial courts of general jurisdiction are its circuit courts; most appeals go to the Court of Appeals, and the seven-member Oregon Supreme Court is the final word on Oregon law. Unlike federal judges, Oregon's appellate judges are chosen by statewide election to six-year terms.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Circuit, Appeals, Supreme - and Oregon voters, not a governor, pick the top court's justices.

questions.question: Oregon citizens draft a new statute setting recycling standards and want to place it on the ballot themselves rather than persuade the Legislative Assembly. What share of the votes cast for governor in the last election must their petition signatures equal?
questions.correctAnswer: 6 percent - the signature threshold for a statutory initiative in Oregon
distractors: 4 percent - the threshold for any citizen measure in Oregon
8 percent - the threshold for statutes and constitutional amendments alike
10 percent - the threshold Oregon sets for all ballot measures
questions.explanation: Oregon measures signature requirements against the total votes cast for governor at the last election. A statutory initiative needs signatures equal to 6 percent of that vote; a constitutional amendment initiative needs 8 percent, and a referendum petition needs 4 percent.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Six for a statute, eight for the constitution, four for a referendum.

questions.question: A different Oregon group wants to amend the state constitution itself through the initiative, adding a new section to the Oregon Bill of Rights. How does their signature target compare with a statutory initiative, and why?
questions.correctAnswer: Higher - 8 percent of the votes cast for governor, because constitutional amendments are meant to be harder to make than ordinary statutes
distractors: Lower - 4 percent of the votes cast for governor, because constitutional rights need fast action
Identical - 6 percent, because Oregon uses one threshold for every measure
Higher - 15 percent, matching Oregon's recall threshold
questions.explanation: Article IV of the Oregon Constitution reserves the initiative power to the people and grades its difficulty: 6 percent of the gubernatorial vote for a statute, 8 percent for a constitutional amendment. The steeper climb for constitutional change mirrors Article V's harder federal path.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Amending the constitution costs two points more: eight, not six.

questions.question: The Legislative Assembly passes an unpopular new fee in June and adjourns. Opponents want the voters themselves to approve or reject the law before it settles in. Which Oregon tool fits, what share of signatures does it need, and how fast must they gather them?
questions.correctAnswer: The referendum - signatures equal to 4 percent of the votes cast for governor, filed within 90 days after the legislative session adjourns
distractors: The initiative - signatures equal to 8 percent, filed within two years of passage
The recall - signatures equal to 15 percent, filed within 90 days of the session
The referral - signatures equal to 6 percent, filed before the governor signs the bill
questions.explanation: The referendum lets voters veto an act of the Legislative Assembly. Opponents have 90 days after adjournment to file petitions bearing signatures equal to 4 percent of the votes cast for governor; if they qualify, the law is suspended and the voters decide it at the next election.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four percent in ninety days: the people's veto runs on a short clock.

questions.question: A measure appears on Oregon ballots not because citizens petitioned, but because the Legislative Assembly voted to ask the voters to decide it themselves - as it must do for any constitutional amendment it proposes. Which process produced this measure?
questions.correctAnswer: A legislative referral - lawmakers refer a measure to the voters, whose approval is required for constitutional amendments
distractors: An initiative - citizens wrote the measure and gathered signatures for it
A recall - voters are being asked to remove an official before the term ends
A referendum - citizens petitioned to veto a law the Assembly already passed
questions.explanation: Oregon lawmakers routinely refer measures to the ballot, and the state constitution requires voter approval for constitutional amendments the Assembly proposes. Referral differs from the initiative (citizen-petitioned) and the referendum (citizen veto of an enacted law).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sometimes the legislature itself hands the question to the voters: a referral.

questions.question: An Oregon county commissioner, eight months into her term, faces a recall drive. Organizers must gather signatures equal to what share of the votes cast for governor in her district, and after an official has served how long can a recall petition first be filed?
questions.correctAnswer: 15 percent of the votes cast for governor in the district, and a recall cannot be filed until the official has served six months of the term
distractors: 6 percent of the votes cast for governor, and a recall may be filed on the first day of the term
25 percent of registered voters, and a recall may be filed after one full year in office
4 percent of the votes cast for governor, and there is no waiting period at all
questions.explanation: Oregon's recall is deliberately demanding: petitions need signatures equal to 15 percent of the votes cast for governor within the official's electoral district, organizers then have 90 days to gather them, and the official must have served at least six months before a petition can be filed. Oregon voters have used it against officials from school boards to the legislature.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteen percent, six months in - recall is Oregon's emergency brake, not a toy.

questions.question: Historians credit one state with pioneering the package of initiative, referendum, and recall in the early 1900s - a package nicknamed after the state itself and copied across the West. Which state, and what is the nickname?
questions.correctAnswer: Oregon - the 'Oregon System,' adopted when voters amended the state constitution in 1902
distractors: California - the 'California Plan,' adopted by its legislature in 1911
Arizona - the 'Arizona Method,' written into its first constitution in 1912
Washington - the 'Puget System,' approved by Congress in 1903
questions.explanation: In 1902 Oregon voters amended their constitution to reserve the initiative and referendum, adding the recall in 1908. The bundle became famous nationwide as the Oregon System, the flagship achievement of the Progressive Era's direct-democracy movement and a model other states copied.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Oregon System: voters seized the pen in 1902 and never gave it back.

questions.question: Election officials from other states travel to Oregon to study an election model the state's voters adopted by citizen initiative in 1998 and first used for a full federal election in 2000 - making Oregon the first state in the nation to run every election this way. Which model are they studying?
questions.correctAnswer: Vote-by-mail - Oregon was the first state to conduct all its elections entirely by mail
distractors: Same-day registration - Oregon lets any resident register at the polls on election day
A top-two primary - Oregon sends the two highest finishers to November regardless of party
Compulsory voting - Oregon fines every registered voter who skips an election
questions.explanation: Oregon voters approved vote-by-mail in 1998 and first used it for a full federal election in 2000, making Oregon the first state to run all elections by mail. Ballots must be received or postmarked by election day, and drop boxes across every county offer an in-person return option.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In Oregon, the ballot comes to the voter - mailbox first, polling place never.

questions.question: An Oregon teenager renews her license at the DMV and weeks later finds she has been registered to vote without ever filling out a registration form - she was given the chance to opt out by mail instead. Which Oregon-first system registered her?
questions.correctAnswer: Motor Voter automatic registration - Oregon's 2015 law (effective 2016) made it the first state to register eligible voters automatically through DMV transactions unless they opt out
distractors: The Oregon System - the 1902 direct-democracy package included automatic registration
The National Voter Registration Act - the 1993 federal law made Oregon register voters at the DMV counter by form
Vote-by-mail - receiving a ballot automatically enrolls the recipient as a voter
questions.explanation: Oregon extended its election-innovation tradition in 2015 with the nation's first automatic voter registration law: eligible citizens interacting with the DMV are registered by default and may opt out afterward. Several states have since copied the model, as they once copied the Oregon System.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: First with mail ballots, first with automatic registration - the DMV does the paperwork.

questions.question: A civics standard asks Oregon students to study the government-to-government relationship between the state and the federally recognized tribal governments within Oregon's borders. Exactly how many such tribal governments are there?
questions.correctAnswer: Nine federally recognized tribal governments
distractors: Five federally recognized tribal governments
Twelve federally recognized tribal governments
Twenty-seven federally recognized tribal governments
questions.explanation: Oregon is home to nine federally recognized tribes: the Burns Paiute Tribe; the Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians; the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community; the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians; the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation; the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs; the Coquille Indian Tribe; the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians; and the Klamath Tribes. Standard HS.C.PI.4 makes their relationship with Oregon required course content.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nine tribal governments, nine partners - count them and remember the number.

questions.question: A student assumes tribal governments are a kind of county created by the State of Oregon and answerable to the governor. A tribal leader corrects her: tribal sovereignty did not come from Oregon at all. What is the correct account?
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal nations are sovereign political entities whose self-government predates the United States; their status is recognized by the U.S. Constitution, treaties, and federal law - not granted by any state
distractors: Tribal governments are federal agencies, created by Congress to administer reservations
Tribal governments are private cultural associations with no governmental authority
Tribal governments hold whatever powers each state legislature chooses to lend them
questions.explanation: Tribal sovereignty is inherent: Native nations governed themselves long before the United States existed, and treaties between tribes and the federal government presuppose nations capable of making them. Oregon deals with the nine tribal governments as governments - the meaning of 'government-to-government' in HS.C.PI.4.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sovereignty older than the state itself - recognized, never granted, by Oregon.

questions.question: In the 1850s, tribes across Oregon signed treaties with the United States ceding vast homelands. A lawyer explains that those documents still matter in court today because of what the tribes kept, not only what they gave up. What did the treaties reserve?
questions.correctAnswer: Reserved rights - by ceding land, tribes retained the rights they did not give up, such as fishing, hunting, and gathering at usual and accustomed places, along with their self-government
distractors: Nothing - the treaties were symbolic ceremonies with no legal force after 1900
State voting rights - the treaties promised tribes seats in the Legislative Assembly
Tax exemptions for all tribal members in every transaction forever
questions.explanation: Under the reserved-rights doctrine, a treaty is not a grant of rights to a tribe but a grant from the tribe: everything not ceded - including off-reservation fishing and gathering rights and self-government - remains with the tribe. Courts still enforce those nineteenth-century promises in the Pacific Northwest today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A treaty is a tribe's grant to the United States, not the other way around.

questions.question: A teacher planning a unit opens the state's Tribal History/Shared History curriculum, a set of lessons Oregon built for grades 4, 8, and 10 and wove into subjects from history to health. Who authored the framework's nine Essential Understandings, and under which 2017 law?
questions.correctAnswer: Oregon's nine federally recognized tribes themselves authored the Essential Understandings, under Senate Bill 13 (2017), which directed the Oregon Department of Education to build the curriculum in partnership with them
distractors: The Oregon Department of Education wrote them alone, under the 2021 civics law
The U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs wrote them, under the Indian Education Act
A national textbook publisher wrote them, under a state procurement contract
questions.explanation: Senate Bill 13 (2017) required ODE to develop a historically accurate, culturally relevant curriculum on the Native American experience in Oregon - in partnership with the tribes, who authored the nine Essential Understandings, from 'Since Time Immemorial' to 'Sovereignty' to 'Treaties with the United States.' The arrangement models the government-to-government relationship the civics standard teaches.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The tribes wrote the understandings; the state built lessons around their words.

questions.question: State agency staff preparing a new water policy that affects the Columbia River are told they cannot simply notify the tribes afterward - consultation must happen first, as a matter of Oregon law. Which framework creates that duty, and when did Oregon establish it?
questions.correctAnswer: Oregon's government-to-government framework, codified after Senate Bill 770 (2001), which directs state agencies to consult and cooperate with the nine tribal governments on policies that affect them
distractors: The Oregon System of 1902, which required tribal approval of all water policy
A 1998 ballot measure that gave tribes veto power over state agency rules
The vote-by-mail law, which requires tribal notice before any agency action
questions.explanation: Executive orders in the 1990s began Oregon's formal government-to-government practice, and SB 770 (2001), now ORS 182.162-168, codified it: agencies must designate contacts, train staff, and consult tribal governments on matters of mutual concern, with an annual summit between the governor and tribal leaders. Consultation is a legal duty, not a courtesy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Consult first, decide second - SB 770 turned respect into a procedure.

questions.question: A student reading Oregon's original 1857 constitution finds a clause barring free Black people who were not already residents from coming to Oregon, holding property, or making contracts - in the only constitution of any state admitted to the Union to contain such a racial exclusion clause. Under which Oregon standard is this document studied, and alongside what?
questions.correctAnswer: HS.C.DP.15 - it is studied for the exclusionary language and intent of the Oregon and U.S. Constitutions, and for the provisions and processes that later expanded and protected civil rights
distractors: HS.C.PI.4 - it is studied as part of the government-to-government relationship with tribal governments
HS.C.IR.8 - it is studied only as an example of efficient government structure
No standard - Oregon removed the clause, so the original text is no longer taught
questions.explanation: The 1857 constitution combined a ban on slavery with a Black exclusion clause voters approved by a wide margin - Oregon was admitted in 1859 as a free state that tried to be an all-white one. HS.C.DP.15 requires students to evaluate that exclusionary language against the rights-expanding amendments that followed, rather than pretend the clause never existed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A free state that tried to exclude: the clause is taught, not hidden.

questions.question: Oregon's exclusion clause outlived its enforcement era by decades, remaining printed in the state constitution long after the Fourteenth Amendment made it unenforceable. In what year did Oregon voters finally delete the language from their constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: 1926 - voters repealed the Black exclusion clause, nearly seventy years after adopting it
distractors: 1868 - the clause was automatically deleted when the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified
1951 - voters removed it as part of the postwar constitutional cleanup
2000 - voters removed the last exclusionary language at the turn of the century
questions.explanation: The clause was a dead letter after the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) and the end of Oregon's exclusion laws, but dead letters stay in constitutions until voters remove them. Oregon voters repealed the Black exclusion clause in 1926; other discriminatory language, aimed at Chinese residents, was likewise repealed by later voter action - a standing lesson in how amendment processes repair constitutions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Unenforceable from 1868, unrepealed until 1926 - removal takes a vote.

questions.question: An Oregon court protects a form of expression even though lawyers concede the U.S. Supreme Court might allow it to be regulated under the First Amendment. The court answers that it does not need federal permission. On what basis?
questions.correctAnswer: The Oregon Constitution's own free-expression clause, Article I, section 8, which Oregon courts interpret independently and have read to give speech protection broader than the federal floor
distractors: The Tenth Amendment, which lets any state court ignore Supreme Court rulings it dislikes
The Oregon System, which lets voters override federal court decisions by initiative
Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause, which imports other states' speech rulings
questions.explanation: State constitutions set floors of their own: a state may protect more liberty than the U.S. Constitution requires, though never less. Oregon courts famously read Article I, section 8's free-expression guarantee independently - in cases such as State v. Henry (1987) - producing protections broader than the federal First Amendment floor.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal rights are a floor, not a ceiling - Oregon's own clause can rise higher.

questions.question: Portland voters adopt a city charter letting their council design its own form of government and legislate on local matters, without asking Salem for a charter. A newcomer asks which Oregon reform lets a city govern itself this way. What is it?
questions.correctAnswer: Municipal home rule - Oregon's 1906 constitutional amendment lets cities adopt their own charters and manage local affairs, within state and federal limits
distractors: The initiative - city voters may legislate directly on any local topic at any time
The referendum - cities may veto any state law by local vote
County home rule only - Oregon cities remain creatures of the legislature entirely
questions.explanation: Oregon was a national leader in home rule: amendments adopted in 1906 let incorporated cities write their own charters and exercise power over municipal affairs. Home rule is another Progressive Era Oregon reform, sitting beside the initiative, referendum, and recall in the state's direct-democracy inheritance.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1906 gave cities their own charters - Salem's permission slip no longer required.

questions.question: Weeks before an election, every Oregon household receives a thick state booklet containing candidate statements, the full text and official explanations of ballot measures, and arguments for and against them bought by any citizen for a modest fee. What is this uniquely Oregon institution?
questions.correctAnswer: The Oregon Voters' Pamphlet - published by the Secretary of State since the early 1900s so voters can study measures at home before voting
distractors: The Federal Register - the national government's daily record of agency rules
The Legislative Assembly's journal - the official record of floor debates
The Oregon Blue Book - the state's almanac of government agencies and officials
questions.explanation: The Voters' Pamphlet began in 1903, a direct companion to the new initiative system: if the people were to legislate, they needed the text, the fiscal estimates, and arguments on every side delivered to their homes. It remains the model of voter information in initiative states - and pairs naturally with vote-by-mail a century later.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The pamphlet is the initiative's instruction manual, mailed to every home.

questions.question: An Oregon high school counselor explains that a student's half-credit of civics cannot be folded into a U.S. history survey course, however good the history teacher is. Which Oregon rule is she applying?
questions.correctAnswer: Senate Bill 513 (2021) - Oregon's standalone Civics credit must be a course addressing only the Civics standards; it may not be blended with other standards
distractors: The Oregon System - voters reserved all course design to ballot measures
Senate Bill 13 - Oregon's Tribal History law forbids combining any two subjects
The Twenty-sixth Amendment - civics must be taught in a student's final semester
questions.explanation: SB 513 (2021) added a standalone 0.5-credit Civics requirement inside Oregon's 3.0 social-science credits, for students first enrolled in grade 9 in 2022-23. The Oregon Department of Education's guidance is explicit: the course must address only the Civics standards and may not blend them with history, geography, or economics - which is why this pack exists as its own test.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Civics stands alone in Oregon: half a credit, no blending allowed.

questions.question: After the 2020 census, Oregon gained something in Washington, D.C., that it had not gained in four decades, while its Senate delegation stayed exactly the same size. What changed, and what does the change illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: Oregon gained a sixth seat in the U.S. House of Representatives (six representatives, two senators) - House seats follow population through reapportionment, while Senate seats never change
distractors: Oregon gained a third senator, because Senate seats follow population growth
Oregon gained a sixth electoral vote, but its House delegation stayed at five
Oregon lost a House seat, illustrating that western states shrink after every census
questions.explanation: Oregon held five House seats from the 1980s until the 2020 census, whose growth figures earned the state a sixth district for the elections of the 2020s. Its Senate delegation stayed at two, as every state's does - the Connecticut Compromise playing out in Oregon's own numbers: eight members of Congress, six by population and two by statehood.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Census growth bought Oregon a sixth House seat; the Senate still reads two.

questions.question: Standard HS.C.IR.8 asks Oregon students to debate the central ideas of the government of the United States and of Oregon side by side. A student's chart lists three branches, a bill of rights, and an elected chief executive on both sides - then adds one row where Oregon differs sharply from the federal design. Which row is it?
questions.correctAnswer: Direct democracy: Oregon voters legislate through the initiative, veto laws by referendum, and remove officials by recall - powers the federal Constitution gives citizens of the United States nowhere
distractors: Term limits: only Oregon limits its chief executive to two consecutive terms
A written constitution: Oregon has one, while the United States does not
A senate: Oregon's constitution gives its legislature two chambers, while the federal Constitution gives Congress only one
questions.explanation: The shared architecture is real - three branches, rights charters, separated powers - which is exactly why the differences teach so much. The federal system reserves lawmaking to representatives; Oregon layers the Oregon System on top of representation, letting voters make, veto, and repeal law and remove officers directly.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same skeleton, extra muscle: Oregon bolted direct democracy onto a republican frame.

questions.question: A federal judge in Oregon serves for life, while an Oregon state judge sitting in the next courtroom must face the voters in a nonpartisan election every six years - and if a state judgeship falls vacant mid-term, the governor's appointee must still win an election to keep the seat. Which value does Oregon's system prioritize that the federal system deliberately trades away?
questions.correctAnswer: Direct democratic accountability of judges - Oregon accepts election pressure on judges as the price of keeping them answerable to the people, while Article III trades accountability for independence
distractors: Judicial supremacy - Oregon judges may overrule the voters at any time
Efficiency - elections are faster than appointments for filling court seats
Federalism in reverse - Oregon copies its judicial selection from Article III exactly
questions.explanation: The contrast is a designed experiment inside one state: federal judges in Oregon are insulated for life under Article III, while Oregon's own judges - including its Supreme Court - are elected statewide to six-year terms, with gubernatorial appointees serving only until the next election. Each system buys one value (accountability or independence) by spending the other.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life tenure on one floor, six-year elections on the next - same building, opposite bets.

questions.question: An Oregon tribe wishes to operate a casino on its reservation. Under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, the casino's Class III gaming cannot simply open - it requires a negotiated agreement with the state. What is that agreement called, and what does negotiating one demonstrate?
questions.correctAnswer: A tribal-state compact - negotiating one demonstrates the government-to-government relationship in action, with the sovereign tribe and the State of Oregon bargaining as governments, not as a business and its regulator
distractors: A home-rule charter - it shows cities and tribes share the same legal status in Oregon
A legislative referral - it shows the Legislative Assembly votes on every tribal enterprise
A treaty amendment - each casino reopens the tribe's nineteenth-century treaty for revision
questions.explanation: IGRA (1988) requires a tribal-state compact for casino-style gaming, negotiated between the governor and the tribe and approved federally. Oregon's compacts with its tribal governments - covering revenue sharing for community benefit and regulatory terms - are the modern, practical face of HS.C.PI.4's government-to-government standard.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A compact is sovereignty at a negotiating table: two governments, one agreement.
